title: Lists and Indexing
content:
What problem does this solve?
One variable holding one value is not enough for an inventory or a party roster. A list stores several values in order under a single name.

Basic syntax
  party = ["Aria", "Rook", "Mira"]
  party[0]

What actually happens
Square brackets create the list. Indexing walks to a position. The first item is at index 0, not 1. party[0] is Aria; party[1] is Rook.

When this is useful
Use a list when you have several related values and you care about their order. Later you will learn how to visit every item. For now, creating the list and reading one position is enough.
concepts: A list holds several values in order under one name

examples.title: Read the first party member
examples.explanation: party[0] is the first name. party[1] would be the second.

common_mistakes: Using index 1 when you meant the first item (that is index 0)
Using parentheses instead of square brackets: party(0) tries to call party like a function

exercises.title: Predict the first item
hints: The number in square brackets is a position, starting at 0.
Index 0 is the first name in the list.
Aria is at position 0, Rook at 1, Mira at 2.

exercises.title: Fix the indexing bug
exercises.prompt: This program is supposed to print the first party member (Aria), but it is wrong. Fix it by indexing into party — do not print the name as a quoted string.
hints: Which index means 'first item' in Python?
Print party at index 0 instead of index 1.

tests.name: party
tests.message: Print an item from party using square-bracket indexing.

exercises.title: Announce the leader
exercises.prompt:
Create a list named party containing "Aria", "Rook", and "Mira" in that order.
Print exactly one line using an f-string:
Leader: Aria

The name must come from party[0], not a hardcoded string.
exercises.starter_code: # Create party, then print the leader
hints: Use square brackets and commas between the string items.
The first item is at index 0.
Print an f-string that inserts party[0] after Leader:

tests.message: Use an f-string so the printed line is built from party[0].

tests.name: party
tests.message: Read the leader with party[0], not a quoted name.
